title: Hosted API circuit-breaker enforcement regression — 2027-07-12 postmortem
content:
Summary:

On 2027-07-12 09:17 UTC the Hosted API experienced a widespread increase in 5xx errors and stalled streaming responses for ~22 minutes affecting ~18% of user requests and several high-throughput customers. Impact included client retries, elevated token costs, and degraded SLAs for a subset of dedicated capacity customers. On-call SRE identified the regression and rolled back an edge-proxy change that reintroduced a stricter circuit-breaker enforcement path.

Primary impact window: 2027-07-12 09:17 — 09:39 UTC
Severity: P0
Services affected: hosted-api edge-proxy, streaming gateway, runtime request dispatcher
Estimated % requests affected: ~18% global 95th percentile 5xx spike, streaming stall rate for active sessions rose to ~12%

High-level timeline (UTC):
- 09:12 - Gradual uptick in error budget alerts (internal observability).
- 09:17 - External customer reports (Slack) + threshold alerts trigger escalation.
- 09:18 - On-call SRE (Aisha) triages; initial hypothesis: autoscaler churn.
- 09:20 - Correlate with edge-proxy deploy rolled 09:10 (PR #812).
- 09:24 - Rolling rollback of edge-proxy begins; temporary mitigation: disable strict cb-enforcement flag.
- 09:30 - Error rates begin falling.
- 09:39 - System stabilized at baseline; monitoring kept for 2 more hours.

Detection:
- Alerts: surge in 5xx (>3x baseline) and streaming timeout rate increase.
- Customer escalations: direct Slack messages from 3 customers experiencing partial downtime.
- Observability: trace tails showing requests failing in edge-proxy with CB_Open and upstream connection refused errors.

Root cause (short):
A change to the edge-proxy circuit-breaker logic (PR #812) introduced a stricter evaluation path that prematurely tripped breakers for mid-latency backend responses. This logic did not account for the new adaptive-batching behavior in the runtime which intentionally increases head-of-line latency for certain batched sequences. As a result, the proxy classified batched requests as unhealthy, opened circuit breakers aggressively, and routed traffic into a small set of fallback paths that became saturated → cascading 5xx and streaming stalls.

Root cause (detailed):
- PR #812 modified the circuit-breaker threshold to evaluate a 95th percentile latency window with a shorter observation period (10s instead of 60s) for faster failover. Change intended to reduce user-facing tail latency on noisy backends.
- Serving runtime had recently shipped adaptive-batching heuristics (canary two weeks earlier) which introduced occasional spikes in per-request service time for specific sequence-length distributions (particularly chat completion prefixes). These spikes are normal and transient but fall into the new short observation window used by the proxy.
- The proxy logic lacked model-awareness: it only looked at tail latency across backend pool without correlating to request-type or batching signals. Mixed traffic caused pooled latency anomalies to look systemic.
- When circuit breakers opened, traffic was routed to a small fallback pool that lacked connection warm-up (no prewarmed KV caches, lower concurrency), producing increased error rates and stream stalls.
- The combination produced feedback loop: more failures → more breaker opens → more routing pressure on fallback → more failures.

Contributing factors:
- Fast rollback window policy: the deploy was automated and rolled forward quickly, but the small observation window made the change high-risk.
- Lack of synthetic coverage: there were no unit/integration tests that simulated adaptive-batching latency profiles against the new CB heuristics.
- Telemetry gaps: proxy metrics did not tag latency by request-bucket (batch size, model family) so correlation required ad-hoc trace joins.
- Fallback pool underprovisioned for sudden reroutes and lacked warm caches for streaming sessions.

Mitigation and immediate remediation taken:
- 09:24 — Flag toggled: cb_short_window=false on edge-proxy cluster (hotfix).
- 09:25 — Temporary request routing throttle enabled to slow down client retries and reduce cascade into fallback pool.
- 09:28 — Prewarm procedure initiated for fallback pool: allocated short-lived KV cache priming jobs for most common prefixes.
- 09:30 — Autoscaler adjusted to add extra fallback nodes; concurrency limits loosened for fallback pool.
- 09:39 — Traffic normalization observed and monitoring confirmed stability.

Why rollback fixed it:
- Restoring the longer observation window prevented transient batched spikes from being classified as systemic, reducing unnecessary circuit breaker openings and allowing normal runtime latencies to resolve within the expected distribution.

Detection + Response timeline notes (lessons):
- The first alert was a generic 5xx surge; it took ~6 minutes to map that to the edge deploy. Our deploy tagging in metrics helped but was not enough — need faster correlation.
- On-call decision to toggle the feature flag was the right move; ability to flip behavior without full redeploy saved ~15 minutes.
- Prewarming fallback caches was effective but manual and slow — should be automated.

Action items (prioritized):
1) Safeguard: Revert PR #812 permanently until mitigations are in place (Owner: Edge team, Liam) — due 2027-07-14.
2) Feature gating: Add model-aware circuit-breaker mode that considers request-bucket tags (batch size, model family) in evaluation (Owner: Edge + Runtime, Riley) — design doc due 2027-07-20.
3) Telemetry: Add latency-by-bucket metrics in proxy (tagging at ingress) so we can alert on per-bucket tail behavior (Owner: Observability, Sofia) — M0 2027-07-19.
4) Testing: Add integration tests that inject adaptive-batching latency patterns into CB simulation harness (Owner: SRE + Runtime QA, Marcus) — target 2027-07-26.
5) Fallback hardening: Ensure fallback pools are prewarmed and autoscale faster; add warm-cache prefill as an automated step on fallback activation (Owner: Platform Eng, Nisha) — target 2027-07-21.
6) Runbook changes: Update hosted-api incident runbook to include "edge-proxy CB rollback" checklist and a short playbook for prewarming fallback caches (Owner: eng-sre, Aisha) — draft 2027-07-15.
7) Deploy safety: Require a canary window of 30m for circuit-breaker heuristic changes plus synthetic traffic with adaptive-batching profiles (Owner: Release Eng, Riley) — policy change 2027-07-18.

Postmortem notes / context for engineers:
- This incident is notable for being a regression where a defensive change (faster CB) interacted poorly with a previous runtime optimization (adaptive-batching). Both changes were reasonable alone but together formed an emergent failure.
- Key takeaway: control-plane heuristics that observe latency must be aware of latent modes of operation (batching, caching) or they will misclassify normal behavior as failure.

Runbook draft excerpt (to be added):
- Symptoms: 5xx surge + streaming stall with traces showing CB_Open at edge.
- Quick checks: verify latest edge-proxy deploys in last 30m; check cb_short_window flag state; examine latency-by-bucket (if available); check fallback pool size and warming status.
- Hotfix steps: toggle cb_short_window=false -> throttle client retry rate -> trigger fallback prewarm -> scale fallback nodes.

Monitoring/Alerts to adjust:
- Add alert for "circuit-breaker open rate by bucket" (warning at 5% for >30s).
- Add dashboard showing cb state, fallback pool utilization, and prewarm queue length.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Should circuit-breaker evaluations be moved into the runtime where we already have model/batch context? Pros/cons discussion scheduled 2027-07-16.
- How to automate fallback prewarm without significant cost? Need cost model for prewarming.
- What additional synthetic traffic patterns are necessary to exercise adaptive-batching cases?

Appendix: data snapshots (links)
- Aggregated error-rate graph: internal graphite link (omitted)
- Trace sample showing CB_Open -> upstream refuseresponse: linked_artifacts[2]
- PR that caused change: https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/812

Notes to self (brief):
- Keep this doc as "draft" until edge + runtime teams sign off on planned fixes.
- Follow up with customers who messaged on Slack with short incident timeline and apology + credits offer where appropriate (CS lead: Maya).

Prepared by: Aisha Patel (on-call SRE)
Reviewers: Liam Chen, Riley Morgan, Sofia Alvarez, Marcus Jung
